background.definition: Rotavirus is a double-stranded RNA virus spread by the fecal-oral route. Infected persons can be asymptomatic, have self-limited diarrhea, or experience a severe gastroenteritis with fever, vomiting, and severe diarrhea that can lead to dehydration and even death. Before vaccine approval in 2006, it was the leading cause of hospitalization for acute gastroenteritis for children in the United States, and globally remains the leading cause of diarrhea mortality in children under 5 years of age.

list.listitem: In 2016 there were an estimated 401.3 cases of rotavirus per 1000 children globally, 118.8 cases per 1000 children in high income countries, and 30.4 per 1000 children in the United States.

The number of deaths in children less than 5 years of age globally has decreased by about 50% from 2000 to 2013, from 528,000 to 215,000 respectively. In 2016, this number decreased further to an estimated 128,500 with most deaths occurring in sub-Saharan Africa. The largest burden of disease remains in countries where vaccination programs are not fully implemented.
In 2016, 7% of diarrheal deaths in the United States and 10% of diarrheal deaths in Canada were attributable to rotavirus.
The rate of hospitalization has decreased from 14/10,000 children in the pre-vaccination era (2000-2006) to 1-3/10,000 children in 2010.

From 2007 to 2011, more than 176,000 hospitalizations, 242,000 emergency department visits, and 1.1 million outpatient visits were averted due to rotavirus vaccine, resulting in over $924 million in health care savings.

In the U.S., where vaccine coverage has plateaued at about 70%, it is estimated 31 deaths were averted due to rotavirus vaccine in 2016. An additional estimated 13 deaths could be averted if vaccine coverage were 100%. Globally, an estimated 28,444 deaths were averted due to rotavirus vaccine in 2016 (27.8% vaccine coverage) with an estimated 83,000 additional deaths that could have been averted with 100% vaccine coverage.

Those undergoing chemotherapy or who are immunosuppressed in the context of organ transplant are particularly susceptible to rotavirus. While these patients generally benefit from the same treatment as non-immunocompromised patients, their disease duration is generally longer.
HIV-infected children are not at higher risk for rotavirus, although adults may be more susceptible.
Rotavirus is a spherical double-stranded RNA virus that causes diarrhea by altering the function of the small intestine in multiple ways.

It infects the small intestinal luminal cells, leading to desquamation and loss of the brush border. This causes loss of digestive and absorptive cells including those needed for digestion of sugars. The virus also encodes an enterotoxin, NSP4, which affects Ca+ transport and causes diarrhea.

Finally, there is evidence the virus affects the enteric nervous systems, causing secretion of fluid and electrolytes. Thus, rotavirus alters the function of the small intestine in several ways to cause a malabsorption and isotonic/secretory diarrhea.
A retrospective study of adults hospitalized with diarrhea showed that patients were more likely to have rotavirus than a bacterial infection if they were immunosuppressed.

Being in contact with an infected child, travel especially to the Caribbean or Central America, and being in the area of an epidemic outbreak may also increase risk for symptomatic rotavirus infection in adults.

list.listitem: Children should be vaccinated according to ACIP guidelines with one of two approved vaccines in the first year of life.A
Promote handwashing programs to prevent episodes of diarrhea. A
Encourage breastfeeding. B
Approved in 2006, RotaTeq is a pentavalent (RV5) oral vaccine given at 2, 4, and 6 months of age.
Approved in 2008, Rotarix (RV1) is a monovalent oral vaccine given at 2 and 4 months of age.
Rotavac is a WHO-approved vaccine in use in India.
Rotavirus vaccine is contraindicated in infants diagnosed with severe combined immunodeficiency or with a history of intussusception.
A recent analysis of randomized controlled trials showed no increase in the rates of intussusception with RV5, RV1, or Rotavac, although this has not yet affected labeling.
Vaccination is recommended for HIV-infected and HIV-exposed infants.
Pediatric rotavirus vaccination is also associated with a reduction in adult rotavirus infections.
Suspect rotavirus in young children presenting with diarrhea, fever, and vomiting; vomiting often precedes the diarrhea. C
Laboratory testing is often unnecessary unless signs and symptom of severe dehydration are present, an outbreak is suspected, or the diagnosis is questionable. C

list.listitem: Suspect rotavirus in children presenting for medical attention with non-bloody diarrhea, fever, and/or vomiting; vomiting often precedes the diarrhea. Rotavirus is more likely when all three present together.

Traditionally, rotavirus often occurred during cooler months (December-May). In the post vaccination era in the U.S., the length of the season has shortened from a median of 26 weeks to 9 weeks, and the season has started later in the year. A biennial pattern has also emerged with alternating years of low and high rotavirus activity.
Rotavirus is most common in young children, especially in those aged 6 to 24 months.
Stools from rotavirus are usually non-bloody.

All children presenting with acute gastroenteritis should be examined for signs of dehydration. The three best tests to evaluate for dehydration are estimated capillary refill time (<2 seconds is normal), skin turgor, and respiratory pattern. Two of the following signs indicate a dehydration level of at least 5%; three or four indicate a level of at least 10%: abnormal skin turgor, absence of tears, prolonged capillary refill, abnormal general appearance.

Adults: Although usually asymptomatic, suspect rotavirus in adults presenting to the hospital with diarrhea especially if they are immunocompromised, older, have infected children, or there is a rotavirus outbreak.
Laboratory tests are needed only if severe dehydration is suspected, confirmation of an outbreak is needed, or to rule out other causes/bloody diarrhea/atypical presentation.
If severe dehydration is suspected, order a metabolic panel to look for electrolyte abnormalities and/or metabolic acidosis.
Order stool tests if diarrhea is persistent, bacterial or parasitic infection is suspected, and/or an outbreak is occurring.
Rotavirus can be detected in the stool through the use of enzyme immunoassays, latex agglutination, and PCR.
Suspect rotavirus in children under 5 years of age presenting with fever, vomiting, and diarrhea.
Examine child for signs and symptoms of dehydration and treat supportively; consider laboratory testing if signs of severe dehydration, an outbreak is suspected, or diagnosis is questionable.
Give supportive care with oral rehydration for mild disease and IV hydration for moderate to severe disease as determined by the patients’ volume status and total output. C
Antivirals such as nitazoxanide appear to reduce the duration of illness in children who are severely ill. B
In nutrient-poor countries or in children who suffer from malnutrition, zinc may benefit children aged 6 months or older. In developed countries, this benefit is not seen. A
Where available, Immunoglobulin Y (IgY) appears to be effective at reducing duration of illness.

For most patients there is no role for drug therapy. In patients with severe disease, one randomized controlled trial found that 3 days of treatment with nitazoxanide decreased the duration of illness by as much as 2 days.
Racecadotril, an antisecretory agent, decreased the duration of diarrhea by a median of 28 hours in severely ill patients in an RCT.

Immunoglobulin Y from egg yolks has been studied since the early 1990's and has several randomized control trials to support the use in Asia, as well as one recent meta-analysis that shows decrease in duration of illness.
Nitazoxanide, racecadotril, and Immunoglobulin Y do not have a clear role in treatment yet, and none has FDA labeling for rotavirus.
To treat volume loss, give supportive care with oral or nasogastric hydration, or with IV fluids for those who are severely dehydrated.

Probiotics with lactobacillus in a meta-analysis trended towards improvement of symptoms. The use of probiotics is reasonable in hospitalized patients; although there is no evidence that it is harmful, there is conflict about its positive efficacy.
Breastfeeding in infants should be continued during illness as immunoglobulins from mother may prevent severe illness.

Treat patients with IV fluids when volume loss is greater than what is possible to maintain with oral rehydration fluid or in patients that are severely dehydrated. When demands of fluid intake surpass those that are manageable by oral ingestion, recommend hospitalization.
Calculator for intravenous fluids: https://www.mdcalc.com/maintenance-fluids-calculations.
For a guide for oral replacement, see .

Patients infected with rotavirus are also at increased risk for neurologic symptoms including seizures. These seizures generally have no long-term complications or need for chronic therapy. Patients with seizures might need acute therapy for their convulsions, but no randomized controlled studies address this.
In a study of 1292 children admitted to a US hospital for rotavirus from 2002 to 2006, 59 had seizures and 34 had no underlying conditions or history of seizures. Of 35, 68% had no fever.
In the developed world, prognosis is uniformly good as the disease process is self-limited, and widespread vaccination prevents much of the illness.B

In the developing world, the prognosis remains poor, and rotavirus remains a leading cause of diarrhea-related deaths in children and infants, mainly due to lack of immunization and poor access to care.B
In adults and older children, the disease process is generally less severe and is not typically a significant cause of morbidity or mortality. C
Older adults may be more susceptible to rotavirus infection. Treatment remains the same.
As mentioned previously, this population has the highest incidence of disease and is statistically more likely to have severe disease.

In this population, appropriate support with oral or IV fluids is of paramount importance in preventing death and complications. Vaccination plays a role in preventing illness in infants and children.
